new_statements.quote: [p.66] In Lhowa, like in Lhasa Tibetan (DeLancey, 2003, p.272) each syllable is intrinsically high or low. In Lhowa, tone (viz., pitch variation) is used to distinguish lexical meaning. Lhowa, like Lhasa Tibetan (DeLancey, 2003,p.272), exhibits a word tone system. The high vs. low tone is distinguished only on the first syllable of a word. [p.68] It is to be noted that like Tibetan, Lhowa is more a pitch-accent language than a true tone language. Lhowa contains word accents in which one syllable in a word or morpheme is more prominent than the others. However, the syllable in which accent is placed is indicated by a contrasting pitch (high vs. low tone). In English, the accentuated syllable is indicated by loudness.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Lhowa has a binary high/low word-tone (pitch-accent-like) system: the tonal contrast is realized only on the first syllable of the word, and non-initial syllables of compounds take predictable melodies (HH, LH, LL, HL). Word prominence ('accent') is said to be marked by pitch rather than loudness; no independent loudness-stress position is stated, though the locus of the contrast is the word-initial syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Compounds and certain derived/inflected verb forms show four tone melodies (HH, LH, LL, HL); no tone sandhi. Authors note an instrumental study is still needed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word/morpheme is the domain of pitch contrast; statements based on citation forms and compounds; impressionistic (no acoustic measurements).
new_statements.first_reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.identity_note: Regmi & Regmi 2024 describe Lhowa/Loke of Upper Mustang (data from Lomanthang and Ghiling speakers) = lowa1242 proper (2021 census name 'Lhopa').
